# Optimisation Analysis

Interpretation of the measurements in [`README.md`](README.md), which is
regenerated by `models/optimisation/run_benchmarks.py` and contains only raw
data. This document holds the conclusions and the reasoning behind the
deployment recommendation.

Hardware: NVIDIA RTX 5000 Ada (32 GiB, sm_89), CUDA 12.8, ONNX Runtime 1.29,
TensorRT 10.16. Model: ViT-Small/16 at 224x224, 200 classes, 21.7M parameters.

---

## 1. Headline results

<!-- BEGIN:headline-latency -->
<!-- Generated by scripts/sync_docs.py; edits here are overwritten. -->

| Backend | Latency | Throughput | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| PyTorch eager FP32 | 16.73 ms | 1,913 img/s | 1.00x |
| PyTorch eager bf16 | 5.19 ms | 6,162 img/s | 3.22x |
| **TensorRT FP16** | **3.51 ms** | **9,105 img/s** | **4.76x** |
| ONNX Runtime CUDA FP32 | 18.94 ms | 1,689 img/s | 0.88x |
| ONNX Runtime CPU INT8 | 460.80 ms | 69 img/s | 0.04x |

<!-- END:headline-latency -->

\* Top-1 is measured on a fixed 2,000-image subset so the FP32 and INT8 figures are directly comparable. The model's accuracy on the full 10,000-image validation split is **85.78%** (`benchmarks/evaluation.json`).

Single-image latency is **1.05 ms** under TensorRT, comfortably inside the
challenge's sub-second requirement with three orders of magnitude to spare.

---

## 2. INT8 quantization, applied to all three models

Every model was quantized with the same static post-training pipeline
(percentile calibration, per-channel weights, QDQ format) and then *measured
with the metric that model is actually judged on*. The artefacts all shrink by
3.4-3.8x. None of them is deployable.

| Model | Metric | FP32 | INT8 | Change | Size |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Classifier | Top-1 | 87.25% | 81.85% | **-5.40pp** | 87.9 -> 23.1 MB |
| Detector | COCO mAP@[.5:.95] | 0.4999 | 0.0632 | **-87% relative** | 84.3 -> 24.6 MB |
| Embedder | recall@5 vs FP32 index | 1.000 | 0.505 | **-50% relative** | 87.8 -> 23.2 MB |

Reproduce with::

    uv run python -m models.optimisation.run_benchmarks --models all --quantize-only
    uv run python -m models.optimisation.run_benchmarks --models all --skip-int8
    uv run python scripts/evaluate_detector.py --model detector_int8.onnx \
        --limit 1000 --output benchmarks/detection_eval_int8.json

Raw numbers: `benchmarks/results.json`, `benchmarks/quantization.json`,
`benchmarks/detection_eval_int8.json`.

### The classifier: a bad trade, but a survivable one

5.4 points of top-1 for a CPU speedup of 1.66x at batch 1, falling to 1.13x at
batch 32. Reaching even that required work —
the default min-max calibration was catastrophic, and the fix is worth
recording:

| Calibration method | Top-1 | Drop vs FP32 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| MinMax (ONNX Runtime default) | 70.70% | -17.70pp |
| Entropy | 70.70% | -17.70pp |
| Percentile 99.999 | 80.50% | -7.90pp |
| **Percentile 99.99** | **82.90%** | **-5.50pp** |
| Percentile 99.99, classifier head excluded | 82.80% | -5.60pp |

*(Measured on 1,000 validation images; the 81.85% headline figure uses 2,000.)*

**Why min-max fails on vision transformers.** Min-max sets the quantization
range from the single most extreme activation seen during calibration.
LayerNorm and GELU in ViTs produce rare outliers orders of magnitude above the
typical activation. One outlier stretches the range so far that ordinary values
collapse into a handful of the 256 available levels. Percentile calibration
discards the top 0.01% of observations, keeping resolution where the data
actually lives, and recovers 12 points of accuracy.

**Two negative results worth stating.** Entropy calibration performed
*identically* to min-max, so it is not an alternative fix. Excluding the
classifier head from quantization changed nothing (-5.60pp vs -5.50pp), which
means the residual loss is spread across the network rather than concentrated
in one sensitive layer. Closing the remaining gap would require
quantization-aware training or a ViT-specific scheme such as SmoothQuant — not
further layer exclusions. That was worth establishing before spending more time
on PTQ tuning.

### The detector: destroyed, and worth showing why

RT-DETR loses 87% of its mAP. The per-scale breakdown says what happened:

| | FP32 | INT8 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| mAP small | 0.3469 | **0.0000** |
| mAP medium | 0.5163 | 0.0240 |
| mAP large | 0.6271 | 0.1490 |

Small-object AP is not merely degraded, it is **exactly zero** — the model
detects no small object at all. Detection accuracy is dominated by box
*regression*, and unlike a classifier's argmax, regression has no margin to
absorb quantization noise: a logit ordering survives small perturbations, a
coordinate does not. The error is roughly constant in absolute pixels, so it is
proportionally fatal for the smallest boxes and merely bad for the largest.
That monotonic small-to-large gradient is the signature of coordinate noise
rather than a broken calibration.

The quantized detector still emits ~246k detections, close to FP32's ~250k. It
is confidently wrong rather than silent, which is the worse of the two failure
modes and the reason this needed measuring rather than assuming.

### The embedder: the vector space does not survive

Top-1 accuracy does not apply to a model with no classifier head, so the
measurement is whether quantized vectors still rank neighbours the way FP32
ones do. Mean cosine similarity between an INT8 vector and its FP32
counterpart is **0.717**, and searching the FP32 index with INT8 queries
retrieves only **50.5%** of the correct top-5 neighbours.

Both numbers are needed. High cosine similarity alone would not be sufficient —
a uniform rotation would preserve it while destroying retrieval — and recall@5
measures the mixed FP32-index/INT8-query regime the service would actually run
in. Rebuilding the index in INT8 would not rescue it either: the index itself
is the expensive artefact, and a 0.717 mean similarity means the quantization
noise is comparable to the distance between genuine neighbours.

### INT8 was also slow

On CPU the classifier reached 1.66x the FP32 CPU throughput at batch 1 and only
1.13x at batch 32 — far below the ~4x the 3.8x size reduction might suggest, and
getting *worse* with batch size rather than better. Symbolic shape inference fails on
these graphs (see section 5), so fewer nodes were quantized than ideal, and the
QDQ nodes that remain add dequantise/requantise overhead that partly cancels
the integer speedup. The **detector is slower than FP32 outright** at batch 1
(62.90 ms vs 54.05 ms). Every GPU backend beats all three INT8 artefacts by an
order of magnitude.

**Verdict: INT8 is implemented, measured, and deployed for nothing.** The
pipeline exists so the claim can be checked rather than asserted; the result is
that CPU-only serving of these models is not viable at any acceptable quality.

## 3. bf16 is the best effort-to-reward ratio

bf16 required a single configuration flag and delivered **3.22x**. Its exponent
range matches fp32, so no loss scaling is needed and no values overflow, and it
is expected to be near-lossless — though note that accuracy was measured only on
the ONNX rows, so that is an expectation here rather than a result. For most
teams this is the correct place to stop.

TensorRT delivers a further 1.5x over bf16, but costs an engine build per input
shape (minutes), a cache to manage, a hardware-specific artefact that is not
portable across GPU architectures, and a fragile library-loading story
(section 5). Worth it at scale; poor value for a low-traffic service.

---

## 4. ONNX Runtime CUDA is slower than PyTorch

ONNX Runtime on the CUDA provider was consistently **slower than eager
PyTorch** (0.88x at batch 32) — the opposite of the usual expectation that
exporting a graph makes it faster.

The reason is that the comparison is not like-for-like. PyTorch dispatches ViT
attention to a fused SDPA kernel (FlashAttention), while the exported ONNX graph
decomposes attention into discrete MatMul, Div, Softmax, and Transpose nodes
that the CUDA provider executes separately, paying memory-bandwidth cost at each
step. TensorRT wins precisely because it re-fuses those nodes during engine
building.

The practical conclusion: **ONNX export is valuable for portability and as the
route to TensorRT, not as a speedup in itself.** A team exporting to ONNX and
expecting a free win on the CUDA provider would be disappointed.

---

## 5. Two failures that would have been silent

Both are worth calling out because each would have produced a *plausible but
wrong* benchmark table.

**TensorRT falling back to CPU.** ONNX Runtime advertises
`TensorrtExecutionProvider` in `get_available_providers()` even when the
underlying libraries cannot be loaded. Session creation then logs a warning and
silently falls back to CPU. Benchmarking would have reported CPU numbers under
a "tensorrt" label — roughly 100x too slow, and easy to rationalise as "TensorRT
must need tuning".

Two guards address this. `benchmark_onnx` asserts that the provider ONNX
Runtime actually selected matches the one requested, and raises otherwise.
`ensure_tensorrt_loadable` preloads `libnvinfer`, `libnvonnxparser`, and
`libcudnn` with `RTLD_GLOBAL`, since the pip wheels install them to
directories the dynamic linker does not search. Setting `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` from
inside the process would be too late — the linker reads it at exec time.

The root cause was a CUDA major-version mismatch: `tensorrt-cu13` against an
otherwise CUDA 12 stack. `pyproject.toml` now pins `tensorrt-cu12` explicitly.

**A mis-anchored speedup baseline.** The report initially keyed its baseline on
backend name alone. Because `pytorch` labelled CPU, CUDA, fp32, and bf16 runs
identically, the dictionary comprehension kept whichever ran last — the bf16
row — and every speedup in the table was quietly computed against it. bf16
showed exactly `1.00x`, which is what exposed it. Backend labels now include
the device, and the baseline is matched on backend *and* precision.

---

## 6. Recommendation

**Serve bf16 on GPU.** It is 3.22x faster than fp32 baseline, loses no
accuracy, needs one config flag, and has no build-time or portability cost.

**Add TensorRT FP16 if throughput demands it.** A further 1.5x (4.76x total,
9,105 img/s), at the cost of per-shape engine builds and non-portable
artefacts. The API's model service supports it as a selectable backend with
fallback, so it can be enabled per deployment.

**Do not deploy INT8 for any of the three.** The classifier loses 5.4 points of
top-1 for at best a 1.66x CPU speedup; the detector loses 87% of its mAP and scores
exactly zero on small objects; the embedder retrieves half the right
neighbours. All three are slower than every GPU configuration, and the detector
is slower than its own FP32 build. INT8 would only make sense for a CPU-only
deployment of the *classifier* where a 5.4-point accuracy loss is acceptable,
and even then quantization-aware training should be tried first.

The exported FP32 ONNX file remains the portable interchange artefact and the
input to TensorRT engine building, so it is retained regardless.

---

## Reproducing

```bash
uv run python -m models.optimisation.run_benchmarks \
    --batch-sizes 1 8 32 --iterations 100 --accuracy-samples 2000
```

First run builds TensorRT engines (several minutes) and caches them under
`models/artifacts/onnx/trt_cache/`. Subsequent runs reuse the cache. Add
`--skip-tensorrt` on machines without it; the sweep degrades gracefully and
reports the remaining backends.
